claims.text: The coating system consists of CoCrFeMnNi HEA and TiN layers.
Reducing the HEA layer thickness increases the density of HEA/TiN interfaces.
HEA/TiN interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion and promote dislocation pile-ups.
Increasing interface density suppresses time-dependent plastic deformation relative to multilayers with thicker HEA layers.
The CoCrFeMnNi layers have a single-phase FCC microstructure.
The initial HEA layers lack significant pre-existing dislocation pinning.
The proposed comparison varies HEA layer thickness between approximately 10 nm and 50 nm while holding TiN layer thickness constant.
Nanoindentation creep testing is proposed at approximately 300 °C, with in situ TEM or high-speed imaging used to observe dislocation dynamics.
The governing structural mediator is the density and configuration of dislocation pile-ups at HEA/TiN interfaces.
Misfit strain and compositional gradients make HEA/TiN interfaces effective dislocation barriers.
Greater interfacial density confines dislocation motion and prevents plastic deformation from propagating over time.
Multilayers with approximately 10 nm HEA layers will have lower creep strain and a later onset of plastic flow than multilayers with approximately 50 nm HEA layers.
Thin-HEA-layer multilayers will exhibit more concentrated dislocation pile-ups at HEA/TiN interfaces.
Thicker-HEA-layer multilayers will exhibit more pronounced dislocation networks and greater creep deformation.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to CoCrFeMnNi/TiN under nanoindentation creep near 300 °C and may not transfer to other HEAs, interlayers, or substantially different temperatures.
The hypothesis would be falsified if thin HEA layers show no statistically significant reduction in creep strain or no enhancement of interfacial dislocation blocking relative to thick HEA layers.
